## AI as a Mathematical Collaborator {.opening-slide}

::: {.eyebrow}
MATH4SDG · UDSM · SATURDAY 21 NOVEMBER 2026
:::

::: {.lead-subtitle}
Build two models. Question the AI. Test the evidence.
:::

::: {.big-question}
**Can we reconstruct missing weather measurements without looking into the future?**
:::

::: {.time-cue}
60-minute student workshop · work alone or in pairs
:::

::: {.notes}
0–2 min. This is a student workshop, not an additional lecture. Students already used JupyterLab. Explain that everyone will build two different models with generative AI, then check whether the claims and results withstand scrutiny. The data are completely synthetic.
:::

## Two stations, incomplete observations

::: {.eyebrow}
THE MATHEMATICAL PROBLEM · 2–6 MIN
:::

::: {.slide-subtitle}
Estimate missing temperatures at A or B using available information.
:::

::: {.small-results}
| Day | A (°C) | B (°C) | Humidity | Wind |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|:--|
| 1 | 28.5 | 28.1 | available | available |
| 2 | **missing** | 29.0 | available | available |
| 3 | **missing** | **missing** | available | available |
| 4 | 30.1 | **missing** | available | available |
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**Allowed:** measurements from today and earlier days. **Not allowed:** later measurements or concealed answers.
:::

::: {.notes}
2–6 min. Same-day observed values at the other station are allowed. The baseline carries forward yesterday's completed temperature when both stations are missing; that previous value may have been estimated. Ask which readings may inform a prediction for day 3. Day 4 is excluded.
:::

## Open the activity in JupyterLab

::: {.eyebrow}
STUDENT ACTION · 6–12 MIN
:::

::: {.activity-steps}
1. Extract the **Saturday student update ZIP** shared by the facilitator.
2. Copy its notebook into the existing **notebooks/** folder and its three CSVs into **data/exercises/**. **Do not replace the folders.**
3. In the **left JupyterLab file browser**, double-click **notebooks**, then double-click **ai_assisted_weather_modelling.ipynb**.
4. Run code cells with **Shift + Enter**. Explore the data, completion rule and baseline.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Keep JupyterLab and your AI assistant open side by side. **No new installation.**
:::

::: {.notes}
6–12 min. Guide students through the local files; they have already started JupyterLab. Facilitators circulate. Show that Shift+Enter runs a cell. Ensure files stay in their original directory structure. Do not ask students to upload partner data to an AI service.
:::

## Ask AI for two different models

::: {.eyebrow}
INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION · 12–32 MIN
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.model-card}
**First model · 10 min**

Ask AI for a simple predictor.

**first_predict_temperature**

Run it. Record the validation MAE.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.model-card}
**Second model · 10 min**

Ask AI for a different mathematical approach.

**second_predict_temperature**

Run it on the **same validation cases**.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Only **earlier training rows** and **one prediction case** may be used. No global data, hidden answers or future observations.
:::

::: {.notes}
12–32 min. Let groups explore different algorithms. Encourage a different model family for the second attempt: linear/ridge regression, SVR, tree, random forest or a simple rule. The notebook supplies each function strictly earlier training rows and one current feature row. AI-generated code must not access globals or CSV files.
:::

## Now challenge your AI assistant

::: {.eyebrow}
CRITICISM AND COMPARISON · 32–43 MIN
:::

::: {.activity-steps}
1. **Compare:** Which mathematical assumptions differ between the models?
2. **Criticize:** How could either fail during missing observations or on new days?
3. **Verify:** Independently check **one AI-generated claim**.
4. **Optional:** Make one change, then measure validation MAE again.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
More complicated—or more convincing-sounding—does not necessarily mean more accurate.
:::

::: {.notes}
32–43 min. Have students request a critique after both models have been constructed. Encourage questions about missing inputs, scaling, leakage, overfitting and long gaps. The result they share should include a checked claim, not simply an improved score.
:::

## Choose first. Reveal second.

::: {.eyebrow}
FINAL TEST · 43–48 MIN
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.model-card}
**1. Lock your choice**

Compare the baseline and both AI models.

Assign **chosen_predict_temperature** to the chosen function.

*Record why you chose it.*
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.model-card}
**2. Test once**

The facilitator reveals the **deobfuscation function**.

Complete **deobfuscation(x)** in JupyterLab.

Compare the final-test MAE with the baseline.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Do not change the selected model after seeing the final-test result.
:::

::: {.notes}
43–48 min. Check students have recorded the selected function and their reason before revealing the deobfuscation formula. Reveal it orally or on the whiteboard only, never in the public repository or pre-distributed slides. Final test values are obfuscated, not securely encrypted.
:::

::: {.eyebrow}
COLLECTIVE EXPERIMENT · 48–60 MIN
:::

| Group | First model | Second model | Chosen | Test MAE | Better than baseline? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|--:|:--|
| 1 | — | — | — | — | — |
| 2 | — | — | — | — | — |
| 3 | — | — | — | — | — |
| 4 | — | — | — | — | — |
| 5 | — | — | — | — | — |
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**What did AI suggest? What did the data support? What did you verify independently?**
:::

::: {.notes}
48–60 min. Collect the five groups' model families, chosen method, final-test MAE relative to the shared baseline, and one critically checked AI claim. Use the table as a blank live template; do not invent scores. A single synthetic dataset does not establish a universally best algorithm.
:::
